sketches.title: Campfire Chain
sketches.premise: Two campers build one campfire in words. On your turn, name a campfire thing that actively deals with what your opponent just added: water douses flame, a shovel buries embers, and roots split a shovel handle. Keep the fire’s story alive until someone offers a useless prop and gets mocked by the host.
sketches.criterion: The Judge accepts only a new, standing campfire object or force that directly changes, contains, uses, or destroys the previous one; merely sitting nearby, surviving it, hiding from it, or making a bigger copy fails.
sketches.move_shape: Say, “I am [thing], and I [plain action] the [previous thing].” Example: “I am rain, and I drown the fire.” The host notes: “A brave little puddle, finally useful.”
sketches.first_card: I am a lit campfire, crackling in the dark.

sketches.title: Tent Trouble
sketches.premise: Two campers assemble and wreck a tent one piece at a time. Each move must be a standing campsite thing that acts on the last one: a pole supports canvas, rain leaks through canvas, and a patch seals the leak. The host has watched enough camping trips to know that confidence is not waterproof.
sketches.criterion: The Judge accepts a thing that physically supports, covers, tears, seals, weighs down, or otherwise directly alters the previous tent-related thing; dodging, merely enduring, and a larger version of the same thing do not count.
sketches.move_shape: Say, “I am [thing], acting on [previous thing] by [action].” Example: “I am a tent peg, pinning the loose canvas.” The host says: “At last, someone brought the one object not already lost in the woods.”
sketches.first_card: I am a canvas tent, stretched beneath the trees.

sketches.title: Trail Mix-Up
sketches.premise: Two hikers pass a single trail-side problem from one solution to the next. Name a standing thing that directly handles what came before: a map guides a lost hiker, a bridge crosses a river, and a flood washes out the bridge. It is not a race; it is a grim little food chain for hikers and their equipment.
sketches.criterion: The Judge accepts only a new trail, travel, or wilderness thing that directly guides, carries, blocks, crosses, breaks, or repairs the previous thing; avoiding it, lasting through it, or offering a bigger relative fails.
sketches.move_shape: Say, “I am [thing], and I [action] what stands.” Example: “I am a compass, pointing the lost hiker toward camp.” The host notes: “Wonderful. North has defeated your entire personality.”
sketches.first_card: I am a lost hiker, turning in circles on the forest trail.

sketches.title: Camp Cooking Carnage
sketches.premise: Two cooks make one campsite meal by forcing each ingredient or tool to deal with the last one. A knife cuts an apple, a pot cooks it, and a lid traps the steam; then someone inevitably proposes ‘a bigger pot’ and learns that volume is not a cooking skill. Every move must do something, not just appear in the kitchen.
sketches.criterion: The Judge accepts a standing camp-cooking ingredient, tool, or force that directly cuts, heats, mixes, contains, cools, spoils, or cleans the previous thing; merely being edible, nearby, tougher, or larger fails.
sketches.move_shape: Say, “I am [thing], and I [action] the [previous thing].” Example: “I am cold water, cooling the hot soup.” The host says: “Bold strategy: weaponize dishwater against dinner.”
sketches.first_card: I am a pot of hot soup, steaming over the camp stove.

sketches.title: Bug-Spray Politics
sketches.premise: Two campers escalate a battle against campsite nuisances. Each turn becomes a standing thing that directly acts on the last one: a mosquito drinks blood, a swat kills the mosquito, and a broom sweeps up the corpse. The host has no sympathy for anyone who loses to an insect, especially in public.
sketches.criterion: The Judge accepts only a thing that directly bites, repels, traps, kills, removes, or blocks the previous campsite pest or countermeasure; hiding, merely resisting, and using a bigger member of the same family fail.
sketches.move_shape: Say, “I am [thing], and I [action] the [previous thing].” Example: “I am bug spray, repelling the mosquito.” The host remarks: “Chemical warfare: because asking the mosquito politely was apparently beneath you.”
sketches.first_card: I am a mosquito, whining beside the sleeping bag.

sketches.title: Campground Court
sketches.premise: Two campers argue over a campsite dispute, but every argument must become a physical camping thing that acts on the last thing said. A posted rule stops loud music, a complaint challenges the rule, and a ranger enforces it; clever mechanisms beat bluster, while pure metaphor gets sent back to the picnic table. The host presides with the weary authority of someone who has read the campground rules and hated every word.
sketches.criterion: The Judge accepts a concrete campsite person, object, or force that plainly stops, changes, exposes, enforces, or removes the previous standing thing; a figure of speech without a real mechanism, mere evasion, endurance, or a bigger copy fails.
sketches.move_shape: Say, “I am [thing], and I [concrete action] the [previous thing].” Example: “I am a ranger, issuing a fine that stops the loud music.” The host says: “A fine argument, if by argument you mean paperwork with a badge.”
sketches.first_card: I am a loud speaker, blasting music through the campground.
